name: Returned Goods Relief (RGR) in the EU
title: Returned Goods Relief in the EU: Claim Duty Relief | TDR
description: Returning goods to the EU? See how Returned Goods Relief (UCC Art. 203) cuts import duty on returns, and how TDR recovers it for you.
hero-description: Goods you exported from the EU are coming home. Make sure you do not pay import duty on them twice.
page-description: Returned Goods Relief (RGR) can provide relief from import duty (and, depending on national VAT rules, import VAT) for qualifying goods returned to the European Union under Union Customs Code Article 203. The key is proving the goods qualify and supporting the claim with the right documentation.

card1.title: Goods return to the EU
card1.description: Customer returns, rejected shipments and other qualifying goods may be eligible for relief from import duty when they come back to the European Union.

card2.title: The proof follows the goods
card2.description: Export records, invoices, transport documents and product identifiers can help demonstrate what left the European Union is what returned.

card3.title: Don't pay duty unnecessarily
card3.description: A well-managed RGR process can help prevent avoidable duty and VAT costs and keep returned inventory moving efficiently.

how-it-works-description: RGR is about proving that qualifying goods meet the requirements for relief from import duty on their return to the European Union. TDR helps connect your export history, returned merchandise and supporting evidence into a clear claim position.

how-it-works-step1.title: Trace the original export
how-it-works-step1.description: Identify when and how the goods left the European Union using export invoices, bills of lading, air waybills, export declarations or other supporting documentation.

how-it-works-step2.title: Prove the goods qualify
how-it-works-step2.description: Match the returned merchandise to the exported goods and confirm that it is returned in the state in which it was exported.

how-it-works-step3.title: Support the duty-free entry
how-it-works-step3.description: Prepare the appropriate RGR claim and supporting declarations and evidence required to substantiate relief from import duty under Union Customs Code Article 203, and VAT treatment where the Member State allows it.

how-it-works-callout.title: Already paid duty on returned goods?
how-it-works-callout.description: Don't assume the opportunity is lost. Keep your import, export and product documentation and let us review whether a recovery opportunity may exist.

eligibility-description: The origin of the goods, timing of the return, condition abroad, export history and available evidence all matter. Start with a quick review of your EU movements.
faq_1_question: What is Returned Goods Relief (RGR) in the EU?
faq_1_answer: Returned Goods Relief is a relief from import duty for goods that were exported from the European Union as Union goods and later come back. Under Union Customs Code (UCC) Article 203, qualifying goods that return within three years, in the state in which they were exported, can be released for free circulation with relief from import duty on application. VAT treatment depends on the rules of the Member State.
faq_2_question: What EU regulation applies to Returned Goods Relief?
faq_2_answer: The principal provision is Article 203 of the Union Customs Code (Regulation (EU) No 952/2013). The relief has to be supported by information showing that the conditions are fulfilled, and delegated and implementing acts set out the detailed rules.
faq_3_question: Do goods have to be manufactured in the European Union to qualify for RGR?
faq_3_answer: No. What matters is that the goods had Union customs status when they were exported, for example because they were released for free circulation in the EU, even if they were manufactured elsewhere. For EU-origin goods, evidence of Union status can strengthen your claim.
faq_4_question: Is there a time limit for returning goods under the RGR provision?
faq_4_answer: Yes. Goods must generally be returned within three years of export from the European Union. The three-year period can be exceeded in special circumstances, as determined by the customs authorities.
faq_5_question: Can goods qualify if they were repaired, repackaged or modified abroad?
faq_5_answer: Relief is granted only if the goods are returned in the state in which they were exported. Whether a repair, repackaging or other treatment changes that state is assessed case by case by customs, so the specific facts matter. Goods that were repaired abroad generally do not qualify as returned goods.
faq_6_question: Does Returned Goods Relief also cover VAT?
faq_6_answer: VAT is a separate question. The EU VAT Directive exempts the re-importation, by the person who exported them, of goods in the state in which they were exported, where those goods are exempt from customs duty. The conditions and procedures are set by each Member State, so check the rules of the country where the goods come back.
faq_7_question: What documentation is required to support an RGR claim?
faq_7_answer: Depending on the circumstances, supporting evidence can include the export declaration, proof of export such as invoices and transport documents, proof that the goods have not been altered, and a returned goods information sheet (INF3) where the Member State requires it. The exact documents depend on the country of re-import and on the origin and value of the goods.
faq_8_question: Is Form INF3 required for Returned Goods Relief?
faq_8_answer: Form INF3 (returned goods information sheet) is commonly used and is issued by the competent authorities in the exporting EU Member State and stamped by customs. However, the documentation required for a particular entry depends on the applicable provision and circumstances. Importers should make sure the documentation supporting the claim is available to customs.
faq_9_question: Do special rules apply in Ireland?
faq_9_answer: In the Republic of Ireland, the audit trail held in the CAS Special Procedures module is used to meet RGR requirements, so no INF3 form is required. Check the current Irish Revenue guidance for your entry.
faq_10_question: Who is responsible for proving that merchandise qualifies?
faq_10_answer: The importer or declarant should be prepared to substantiate the claim to customs authorities. Relief is not applied automatically: the importer must be able to demonstrate that the goods meet the requirements, or pay the applicable duty and VAT.

faq_11_question: Can non-EU origin goods that were previously imported into the EU qualify?
faq_11_answer: Yes, in certain circumstances. UCC Article 203 applies to goods that were exported as Union goods, which can include goods of non-EU origin that had been released for free circulation in the EU, provided they come back within three years in the state in which they were exported and the documentary requirements are met.
faq_12_question: What if I already paid duty on returned goods?
faq_12_answer: The opportunity may not be lost. Keep your import, export and product documentation and contact TDR so we can review whether a recovery opportunity exists. Time limits apply to repayment claims.
faq_13_question: Is Returned Goods Relief the same as duty drawback?
faq_13_answer: No. Returned Goods Relief gives relief from duty when qualifying goods are re-imported. Duty drawback is a refund of duty that was previously paid. See our EU duty drawback page for the refund route.
conditions-title: When does Returned Goods Relief apply in the EU?
conditions-intro: Returned Goods Relief under Article 203 of the Union Customs Code relieves import duty on goods that left the EU as Union goods and later come back. For eCommerce retailers, this is typically a customer return from outside the EU.
conditions-item1: The goods were exported from the EU as Union goods.
conditions-item2: They are returned within three years of export (the period can be exceeded in special circumstances).
conditions-item3: They are returned in the state in which they were exported.
conditions-item4: The relief is requested by the declarant and supported by information showing the conditions are met.
conditions-item5: Part of an earlier export can qualify; the whole shipment does not have to return.
conditions-callout-description: VAT is handled separately from customs duty. The EU VAT Directive exempts re-importation by the person who exported the goods, in the state they were exported, where the goods are exempt from customs duty, and each Member State sets its own procedure.
ecom-title: Returned Goods Relief for eCommerce returns
ecom-intro: Customer returns from outside the EU often arrive as many small parcels. Each one needs to be linked to the original export from the EU, and the evidence has to be ready when customs asks for it.
ecom-list-title: Where eCommerce claims usually go wrong
ecom-item1: The returning parcel cannot be matched to the original export.
ecom-item2: Export documents are held by different parties (carrier, marketplace, 3PL) and are hard to retrieve.
ecom-item3: Goods are returned in a different condition from the one in which they left.
ecom-item4: Relief is not claimed at import, so duty is paid without anyone checking whether the return qualified.
ecom-item5: Member State practices differ and the declarant does not know which documents are expected.
ecom-description: TDR matches returns to exports, prepares the claim and supporting evidence, and reviews whether duty already paid can be recovered.
ctx-title: EU customs changes in 2026: why returns deserve a closer look
ctx-intro: From 1 July 2026, the EU applies a temporary flat customs duty of €3 per item category on consignments valued at €150 or less, until 1 July 2028. Product identifiers become mandatory from 1 November 2026 for affected low-value consignments.
ctx-description: This applies to goods entering the EU from outside, not to the relief for returned Union goods described on this page. But as border costs rise, retailers are looking more closely at every duty cost, including those on returns.
